prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of prose and poetry that builds from memory, the body and dream a densely patterned, unmistakable inner cosmos in Romanian.

statement.case_for: My opening view stands after reading my colleagues' openings. On the supplied entry and public knowledge, Cărtărescu has a voice that is hard to confuse with any other writer's. Blinding and Solenoid make memory, the body and dream into a sustained metaphysical project with real architectural and imagistic ambition. His poetry gives the prose its lyric and imagistic density, so the oeuvre is more than a few very large novels. His career runs from poetry in the 1980s to major late novels along a coherent trajectory, which bears on sustained quality. Under common criteria (distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, depth, significance across the body of work) he is the candidate for whom I can make the strongest case. The question the committee must ask is whether a voice exists in this work 'and nowhere else', and I think it does. All six openings place him in the top three, and I treat that only as a signal that the arguments deserve a close hearing, not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the case rests heavily on translation of prose whose effect depends on sentence-level density, rhythm and Romanian-language texture. I cannot verify how much of that survives. The very large, self-referential novels may also vary in quality across their length, with a risk of excess or repetition, so the citation must rest on the whole oeuvre, including the poetry and shorter fiction, and not on the biggest books alone. My knowledge of the earlier poetry and shorter work is less detailed than of the major novels. Carson's case, by contrast, is conceptually easier to state in terms of formal reinvention, and I should not let the scale of Cărtărescu's books substitute for a judgment of quality.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first for a distinctive voice and formal invention tied to real intellectual depth and emotional force. She also flags that Carson's translations of ancient texts sit at the edge of what counts as original literary work, and that book-object works may be lost in a text-only reading. She ranks Cărtărescu second and names translation of his dense Romanian prose as the main uncertainty.
responses.response: I agree with her point about translations: the credit for Carson should rest on the original works, Autobiography of Red and Nox among them, and not on the classical versions. I also accept her translation caveat about Cărtărescu as my own. Where I differ is on the central achievement. Carson's range across scholarship, lyric, essay and object-book makes a single defining achievement harder to name, whereas Cărtararescu's project can be stated in one sentence and sustained across decades. That is a difference in how clearly the oeuvre coheres, not a finding that one invention is greater than the other.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Carson first and judges her work against the will's 'ideal direction' as offering sustained intellectual and linguistic daring with lyric intensity. He notes that her allusiveness may narrow the readership and that the hybrid books are demanding. He also warns that the very large works of Cărtărescu risk excess or repetition and that translation coverage of the poetry is incomplete.
responses.response: His warning about excess is the one I take most seriously, and it is why I want the committee to read across the poetry and shorter work before treating the large novels as the whole case. I do not think the difficulty of Carson's allusive method counts against her. Difficulty is not a defect in itself, and the same applies to Cărtărescu. The test for both is whether the demanding form carries real imaginative and intellectual weight. For Cărtărescu I believe it does, and I would want a close reading of the later novels to confirm that the late work extends the project and does not merely restate it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He sees the strength of Cărtărescu in the coherence of a large inner world built through linguistic and structural invention. He raises the question of how Carson's genre-crossing work fits the will's wording, and says the translation and classical-scholarship component is hard to separate from original creation.
responses.response: We reach the same first choice by similar reasoning, so I will use the exchange to test it. Olsson's point that Carson's classical-scholarship component is hard to separate from original creation is a fair qualification, and it is part of why I rank her third and not first. Where I would press him is on the shared reliance on translation. If we both accept that the Romanian texture is beyond our direct assessment, we should say so explicitly in any citation and not let agreement between us stand in for verification.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She puts Michon third, and notes that his small volume makes the case on breadth thinner than for prolific candidates and that the style is hard to translate. She sees Cărtărescu's recognition as growing, which supports the timing.
responses.response: I rank Michon second on language and compression, and I share her concern about the slim corpus. The criterion is the whole oeuvre, and extraordinary density does not fully answer a question about breadth. That is the main reason I keep Michon as an alternative and not my first choice. I would qualify her remark about timing: growing recognition is not evidence of literary merit, and I would not use it as an argument for Cărtărescu. The argument has to be made from the work.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She notes that Cărtărescu's late novels extend his visionary vocabulary and not merely repeat it. For Wright, she says the work addresses historical and political subjects through formal invention, and that political significance must not stand in for literary merit.
responses.response: I agree with her principle on Wright, which should hold for every candidate: Wright is judged on form, voice and sustained quality, not on the symbolism of an Indigenous sovereignty theme. On that basis I find the corpus of a few major novels too small to establish sustained quality yet, which is why I place her below Michon and Adonis. I would welcome her evidence for the claim that Cărtărescu's late work extends the earlier vocabulary, since this is exactly what I cannot confirm and what the case for him needs.

uncertainties: Original-language texture and sentence-level patterning of the Romanian prose cannot be assessed directly. The case rests on translations of uncertain fidelity.
Whether the very large novels sustain quality across their length, or fall into excess or repetition, needs a close reading of the full corpus.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's early poetry and shorter fiction in translation is incomplete, and my knowledge of those works is less detailed than of the major novels.
How the committee should separate Carson's original works from her classical translations and versions for citation purposes remains unresolved.
Whether Michon's small corpus is sufficient for a prize defined by the whole oeuvre, and how much weight intensity should carry against breadth, is an open question.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records Ellen Mattson's own practice as historical and psychological fiction, but that is context and not evidence of a connection to any shortlisted writer. No relationship to a candidate is recorded.
